743.title: When sakhis differ
743.hook: traditions sometimes tell the same story in different places; the lesson usually stays the same
743.howItsDone: Sikh teachers telling a sakhi may note that tellings differ, and the Guru Granth Sahib, not any janamsakhi, is treated as the Guru and final authority.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhumia's promises: three small vows that turned a robber around. Your line was promises change us. Did your one promise hold? Day seven hundred forty-three.

At a family dinner, two cousins start telling the same story about their grandfather. One says it happened at the train station. The other says no, it was the market, and it was raining. They argue about the rain for five minutes. Then someone at the end of the table says: does it matter? He gave the man his coat either way. Everyone goes quiet, because that was the whole point of the story. The janamsakhis have dinners like that too. Today: when sakhis differ.
screen: `THE STATION, OR THE MARKET?` → `HE GAVE THE COAT EITHER WAY.` → `THE JANAMSAKHIS HAVE DINNERS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: This block began with the janamsakhis and their families: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's reflective one, the illustrated pages. They don't always agree. A sakhi set in one town in one collection may turn up in another town somewhere else. You've already met it on this path. Tellings place Mardana's death in different places. They differ on what the king did with Bhumia the robber. A detail added in one is missing in another. How do you hold that? Go back to what a sakhi is. We said it at the start: truth carried in the shape of a story. A news report lives or dies by where and when. A sakhi lives by what it teaches. So watch what stays put when the details move. Mardana refuses a tomb, wherever he dies. Bhumia's three promises hold, whatever the king decides. The lesson stays. The differences have their own value, too. Historians compare tellings to learn which material looks older and how stories traveled. That work isn't an attack on the sakhis; it's a kind of care for them. And the differences leave room for humility. A teller who says, in some tellings it was here, in others there, is being honest. Sikh tradition gives its highest authority to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to any janamsakhi, so the stories can differ without the ground moving.
screen: `THE JANAMSAKHIS DON'T ALWAYS AGREE.` · `A SAKHI LIVES BY WHAT IT TEACHES.` · `DETAILS MOVE; THE LESSON STAYS.` · `HONEST ABOUT DIFFERENCES.` · then, large: `THE LESSON STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one question open. Pick a story you know two ways: a family story, a news story, a sakhi from this month. Where do the tellings part? For the sit, don't decide which is right. Just let both stand side by side, and ask what they share. Notice what it's like to leave the question open instead of winning it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
When sakhis differ. Tellings of Nanak's life that place a story in different towns or add different details, while the lesson they carry stays the same.
Your line: the lesson stays. Today, when someone tells a story differently from you, ask what it teaches before you correct the details. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: Painted sakhis
744.hook: sakhis became paintings, murals and later posters in Sikh homes
744.tomorrow: Telling a sakhi to a child
744.howItsDone: Sikh homes and gurdwaras may display paintings and prints of scenes from the Gurus' lives as reminders of the stories, while the bow in the gurdwara is made to the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when sakhis differ: the details move between tellings, the teaching holds. Your line was the lesson stays. Which question did you leave open? Day seven hundred forty-four.

In a living room in Birmingham, or Fresno, or Ludhiana, there's a framed picture above the sofa. An old man with a white beard sits under a tree. On one side, a younger man holds a stringed instrument. On the other, a man waves a whisk over him. A child in that house has looked at it every day since before she could read. Ask her who they are, and she'll tell you. Nobody sat her down for a lesson. The wall did it. Today: painted sakhis.
screen: `A PICTURE ABOVE THE SOFA.` → `AN OLD MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE WALL TAUGHT HER.`

segments.voice: On day seven hundred twenty-six we met B40, a book with a painting beside each sakhi. A book like that sits on a shelf, and someone has to open it. Today the pictures leave the book. Sakhis went up on walls: murals painted inside gurdwaras and old houses, showing Nanak on the road, at the river, with the yogis on the mountain. Later came printed pictures, posters and calendars, cheap enough to hang in any home. That changes how a picture teaches. A page is seen when you sit down to read it. A wall is seen over and over without trying: on the way to breakfast, in the middle of an argument, on a sick day on the sofa. The girl in that living room never had a lesson. She had years of passing by. Now look closer at her picture. The man with the whisk is Bhai Bala, the companion from the Bala tellings, the one historians still discuss. A print has no footnotes. It quietly carries one telling's choices into the house, and its faces are each artist's own imagining. So yesterday's habit works on walls too: ask what the picture knows, and which telling it comes from. Sikh teachers add a caution here. A picture is a reminder of a story, not something to bow to. In the gurdwara, the bow goes to the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. The picture on the wall points; it doesn't receive.
screen: `FROM SHELF TO WALL.` · `SEEN EVERY DAY WITHOUT TRYING.` · `THE PICTURE CARRIES A TELLING.` · `A REMINDER, NOT AN OBJECT OF WORSHIP.` · then, large: `PICTURES TEACH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a picture on your wall. Any picture: a family photo, a print, a poster, a child's drawing on the fridge. If nothing's on your wall, use the lock screen on your phone. For the sit, just look. What moment did someone choose to keep? What does it teach anyone who walks past it every day? Let your eyes rest on it, and let the story come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Painted sakhis. Stories of the Gurus carried in pictures: on book pages, on walls, and in printed pictures in homes.
Your line: pictures teach. Today, notice one picture you pass every day, and ask what it has been teaching you without a word. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: Telling a sakhi to a child
745.word: Telling a sakhi to a child
745.hook: sakhis were first told aloud to children and sangats
745.howItsDone: Sikh families tell sakhis to children at home, and sakhis are told in gurdwaras in katha and in children's classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, painted sakhis, stories that moved from pages to walls to living rooms. Your line was pictures teach. What was the picture you pass every day teaching you? Day seven hundred forty-five.

Again. Tell it again. Bedtime, the same story for the fourth night running, and a small voice under the blanket wants it once more. The child already knows how it ends. That isn't the point. The point is hearing it from you, in your voice, with the pause in the same place. Before sakhis were written in collections or painted on walls, they lived like that: spoken aloud, to children at home and to the sangat, the gathered community. Today: telling a sakhi to a child.
screen: `AGAIN. TELL IT AGAIN.` → `THE SAME PAUSE IN THE SAME PLACE.` → `SPOKEN BEFORE WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Take a sakhi from the last few days and try it out loud. The two villages works well. Start with the road: Nanak and Mardana, dusty and hungry, walking into a village at dusk. Let the doors close. Let somebody laugh. Then the blessing: may you stay settled. Pause. Then the kind village, the bread for the road, and: may you scatter. And now, the best part, let the child be Mardana. Wait. That's backward! Good tellers find the moment. A sakhi like this has a turn, the place where the surprise lives. Slow down there. Rush everything else if you need to. They let the questions in. Mardana speaks up in these stories, and his objections can be the child's. When a child says that's not fair, the story is working. And they tell it true. Back on day seven hundred twenty, we said a story lives because someone tells it well and truly. With a child, that means saying tradition says when it's tradition, and it's fine to say, I don't know, some people tell it differently. One more thing: don't explain it to death. Say the lesson once, plainly, then stop. Unkindness stays where it is; goodness travels. Let the child carry the rest. That's how sakhis reached the sangat: not as a lecture, but as a voice in a room, and someone who'll ask for it again.
screen: `TRY IT OUT LOUD.` · `SLOW DOWN AT THE TURN.` · `LET THE CHILD BE MARDANA.` · `SAY THE LESSON ONCE, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `PASS IT ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one sakhi aloud. If there's a child near you, or a friend, tell it to them today. For now, use the sit to rehearse. Choose the sakhi: the two villages, the boy and the kindling, Bhumia's promises, or one you love. Find its one turn. Say it under your breath, beginning, turn, lesson, in your own words. No script. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath once you're done. The bell holds the time.
Telling a sakhi to a child. A story of the Gurus spoken aloud: slow at the turn, open to questions, true about what's tradition, with the lesson said once.
screen: `TELLING A SAKHI TO A CHILD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pass it on. Today, tell one story you love to someone younger than you, and if they say again, tell it again. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: The sakhis close
746.hook: the travels, the tests, the laughter and the lessons
746.howItsDone: Sikhs return to the sakhis of Guru Nanak's life in katha, at gurpurab celebrations and at home, and families have favorites they tell again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, telling a sakhi to a child: slow at the turn, the lesson said once. Your line was pass it on. Who did you tell a story to? Did they ask for it again? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Boiling oil gone cool. A dead pipal tree turning green. Bitter soapnuts that tasted sweet. A pot cooking on an eclipse day while the crowd shouted. A boy watching kindling catch. A robber setting down treasure because he'd tasted salt. That's a lot of road for twenty-five days. This block opened the janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, and walked through them one sakhi at a time. Today we stop at the end of the road and look back. The sakhis close.
screen: `OIL GONE COOL. SOAPNUTS MADE SWEET.` → `A ROBBER SETS DOWN THE TREASURE.` → `LOOKING BACK DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the books. We met the families of janamsakhis: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's thoughtful one, the illustrated pages. We learned how to read a sakhi: not a news report, but truth in the shape of a story. Then the people around Nanak. Mata Sulakhni, who kept the home going. Sri Chand, who chose a different path. Parents in Talwandi asking him to stay. Then the travels and the tests. Kauda and the oil. Mardana bewitched and sung free. Bitter fruit made sweet. The yogis' seat. Cooking at the eclipse. The learned man of Benares. Farid's verses kept at Pakpattan. The king of the island, waiting. Then endings and beginnings. Mardana's last song, and the rabab handed on. A boy by the fire who became Baba Buddha. Two villages, settle here, scatter there. Bhumia's three promises. And last, how the sakhis live: differing in the details while the lesson stays, painted on walls, told aloud to children. Look across all of it and a pattern shows. In these sakhis, the tests aren't won by force. The oil cools, the robber keeps his word, the pandit listens to a song. And there's laughter in it, too: a Guru blessing the rude village to stay home. Tomorrow a new block begins, and the voices change. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of Bhagats, holy poets from different backgrounds. We met Kabir and Farid already. Next, the Bhagats in their own voices.
screen: `THE BOOKS, AND HOW TO READ THEM.` · `THE PEOPLE AROUND NANAK.` · `TRAVELS, TESTS AND ENDINGS.` · `HOW SAKHIS LIVE ON.` · then, large: `MY FAVORITE SAKHI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your favorite sakhi. Let them pass by in the sit, one at a time, like pictures on a wall. The oil. The soapnuts. Mardana's rabab. The boy and the kindling. The two villages. Bhumia and the salt. Don't think too hard. Notice which one you keep coming back to, the one that tugs. That's yours. Then ask it one question: what do you know that I need today? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
The sakhis close. The end of this block of Nanak's life-stories: the travels, the tests, the laughter and the lessons, with one sakhi chosen to keep.
Your line: my favorite sakhi. Today, tell someone which sakhi you chose and why, in three sentences or fewer. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Fifteen voices
747.hook: Kabir, Farid, Namdev, Ravidas, Trilochan, Beni, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas, Jaidev and Bhikhan
747.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the hymns of the bhagats are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib with the same honor as the Gurus' hymns, and the bhagat hymns carry their singers' names.

segments.voice: Yesterday the sakhis closed, and your line was my favorite sakhi. Which one did you choose, and did it surprise you? Today a new stretch of the road begins. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

Kabir. Farid. Namdev. Ravidas. Trilochan. Beni. Dhanna. Sain. Pipa. Sadhna. Ramanand. Parmanand. Surdas. Jaidev. Bhikhan. Not one of those names belongs to a Sikh Guru. Some were Hindu devotees, some came from Muslim families, and by their own words several worked with their hands: a weaver, a man who carried dead cattle, a cloth printer. And yet their hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru. For the next stretch of days we meet these singers one by one. Today, all of them at once.
screen: `FIFTEEN NAMES, NO GURU AMONG THEM.` → `WEAVERS, PRINTERS, DEVOTEES.` → `INSIDE THE GURU'S OWN BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call them the bhagats, the devotees. Tradition says that when Guru Arjan gathered the hymns that became the Granth, he set the words of these saints beside the words of the Gurus. Where their hymns appear, they come at the end of a raag's section, after the Gurus' own. And there they are, under the same musical headings, read in the same voice by the same granthi, bowed to the same way. There's a hymn in Raag Asa, at the start of Bhagat Dhanna's hymns, that is almost a roll call. It tells how Namdev, a calico printer worth half a copper coin, became worth a fortune. How Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. How Ravidas, who carried dead cattle, let go of the world's pull. How Sain, the barber, became a devotee. And Dhanna, a farmer, hears all this and gets up to give his own life to devotion. Look at that list. It doesn't open with a king or a priest. It opens with working people, named by their trades. The bhagat hymns sign themselves, too. Listen and you'll hear Kahu Kabir, says Kabir, or Kahi Ravidas, says Ravidas, near the end. The voices stay distinct. Their accents differ, their languages differ, some lines sound like a village and some like a court. And yet in the Sikh telling there isn't a front section for the Gurus and a back shelf for guests. The whole book together is the Guru. That's today's line: fifteen voices, one guru.
screen: `THE BHAGATS: THE DEVOTEES.` · `AT THE END OF A RAAG.` · `A ROLL CALL OF WORKING PEOPLE.` · `THE HYMNS SIGN THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `FIFTEEN VOICES, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say three names slowly. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Pick any three of the fifteen. Kabir, Farid, Ravidas, or any that catch your ear. Say the first one, quietly or in your head, and let it ring out like a bell. Wait. Then the second. Then the third. Don't try to know anything about them yet. Just let each name be a person who once sang. If you pray, you can follow the three names with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Fifteen voices. The bhagats, saints from many castes and backgrounds, whose hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.
Your line: fifteen voices, one guru. Today, notice one voice you usually skip past, a coworker, a neighbor, a cousin, and hear it out to the end. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: The weaver of Benares
748.hook: Kabir, a weaver of Kashi, sang the Lord's name in the plain speech of the street
748.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Kabir's hymns in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, and his signature 'says Kabir' is heard in gurdwaras in raag after raag.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fifteen voices, and your line, fifteen voices, one guru. Which three names did you say slowly, and did one of them stick? Today we sit down beside the first. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

Clack. Shuttle across. Clack. Beater down. Clack. Across again. In the old city of Kashi, the city also called Benares or Varanasi, a man sits at a loom set into the floor, feet on the pedals, hands throwing the shuttle back and forth, all day. Thread in, cloth out. Somewhere in that rhythm, he starts to sing. And the songs he made at work, or so tradition tells it, travel further than any cloth he ever sold. Some of them end up inside the Guru Granth Sahib. His name is Kabir, and today's word is what he did for a living.
screen: `CLACK. SHUTTLE ACROSS.` → `A LOOM IN KASHI.` → `A MAN SINGS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Julaha. A weaver. It's not a title somebody gave Kabir later. He uses it about himself. In a hymn in Raag Asa, Kabir speaks to a Brahmin and says, in plain words: you are a Brahmin, and I am a weaver of Kashi. Then he asks the man to grasp what he's saying. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't hide the trade. A weaver in that world was a working man, and some looked down on the work. Kabir sets it right there in the hymn, next to his name, like a signature. Tradition says he grew up in a Muslim family of weavers, and the hymns sing of Ram and Hari, of Allah and the One beyond every name. Sikhs honor him as a bhagat, a devotee of the One. The second thing to hear is his language. Kabir's hymns in the Granth often sound less like a temple or a court than like a lane in a market. Pots, threads, cows, a dog, a mother, a loom. He took the things in front of him and made them carry God. And here's the turn. Yesterday's roll call in Raag Asa said Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. And yet the loom never leaves his songs. The work becomes the picture. Whatever he sings about the Lord, he often sings it with a weaver's hands. So that's today's line. Not a hymn written far from work, but a weaver's song: devotion sung at the level of the shuttle and the thread.
screen: `I AM A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE TRADE, SET BY HIS NAME.` · `THE SPEECH OF THE MARKET LANE.` · `THE LOOM NEVER LEAVES HIS SONGS.` · then, large: `A WEAVER'S SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your work as a song. Pick one plain task you'll do today anyway. Dishes, typing, folding, driving. Settle, and breathe. Now find the rhythm inside it. A plate in, a plate out. A key, a key, a space. Don't add music. Just notice the beat that's already there, and let your breath ride on it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru sit on that beat, once with each round. The bell holds the time.
Julaha. A weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, a weaver of Kashi, set beside his name in the Guru's book.
Your line: a weaver's song. Today, do one ordinary job slowly enough to hear its rhythm, and let it be your song for those few minutes. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: Warp and weft
749.hook: Kabir pictures the world as cloth on the Lord's loom, and the body as the place the weaver comes home
749.howItsDone: Sikhs sing and reflect on Kabir's loom hymns in kirtan and katha, reading the weaver and the cloth as pictures of the Creator, the world and the soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, julaha, a weaver, and your line, a weaver's song. Did one plain job find its rhythm? It's the end of a week that closed the sakhis and opened the bhagats. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

Pull a thread from the hem of your sleeve and you'll find it isn't alone. Every piece of cloth is two sets of thread. One set is stretched long and tight on the loom before anything begins. That's the warp. The other runs across it, over and under, carried by the shuttle. That's the weft. Neither one is cloth by itself. Only crossed do they hold. Kabir knew this the way a cook knows salt. And in one hymn he takes the whole loom, frame and thread and shuttle, and hangs the universe on it. Today: warp and weft.
screen: `TWO SETS OF THREAD.` → `THE WARP, STRETCHED LONG.` → `THE WEFT, CARRIED ACROSS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa. It begins with a riddle. Nobody, Kabir says, knows the secret of the Weaver, who has stretched out the whole world as his warp. So God here is not a king on a throne. God is a weaver, and the world is the long thread on the frame. Then Kabir widens it. The earth and the sky are made into the loom. The sun and the moon move across together, like the shuttles going back and forth. You can almost hear it: day, night, day, night, the weft running across the warp. There's even a little jab in it. While you sat listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, he says, I stretched out this much of my warp. In other words: I was working, and the work was teaching me. Then the hymn turns inward. The weaver, Kabir sings, came to know his own home, and recognized the Lord right inside the body. The loom outside became the loom within. And the hymn ends at the end of a life. When the loom is broken, he says, the weaver merges thread into thread. The cloth comes off the frame, and the thread goes back to the thread it came from. Some readers hear in this the soul returning to the One it was always part of. Nothing in the picture is wasted, and nothing is separate. That's the word for the week's end: woven. Not stacked side by side. Crossed, over and under, until it holds.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS THE WEAVER'S SECRET.` · `EARTH AND SKY, THE LOOM.` · `THE LORD, INSIDE THE BODY.` · `THREAD MERGES INTO THREAD.` · then, large: `WOVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look closely at a piece of cloth. Your sleeve, a towel, a scarf, the knee of your jeans. Settle, and breathe. Bring it close to your eyes. Find the threads running one way, then the threads crossing them. Follow one thread as far as you can before it disappears under another. Notice that it never stops being itself, and never stops holding the others. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you trace it. The bell holds the time.
Warp and weft. The long threads and the crossing threads. In Kabir's hymn, the world stretched on the Lord's loom, with sun and moon running across.
Your line: woven. Look back over this week, the sakhis you chose and the voices you met, and notice one thread that crossed another and held. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, a weaver, and others sit listening to learned texts. you want to sing about God and the world. what picture do you reach for?
options: a palace with its king.
the loom you sit at every day.
a battlefield with two armies.
fork.reveal: the loom: earth and sky the frame, sun and moon the shuttles, the world the warp.

trapdoor: what you thought: warp and weft are just weaving terms.
what it means: in Kabir's hymn the world is the Lord's warp, and day and night run across it like weft.
what a scholar hears: the hymn ends with the broken loom and thread merging into thread, which many readers hear as the soul returning to the One.
